Padmapurāṇa
or Pādmapurāṇa. one of the eighteen mahāpurāṇas; prob. not later than 3rd or 4th Cent. A. D.; for the dates of the different sections see A. Chatterjee, Padmapurāṇa-A Study p.. 38. 58. 64. 80; revealed by Hari to Brahmā; text mentions its extent a. 55000 verses; divided into five khaṇḍas -- Sṛṣṭi, Bhūmi, Svarga (Ādi an. Brahma), Pātāla an. Uttara; several recasts of this Purāṇa appear to have been made. For details see R. C. Hazra, Purāṇic Records on Hindu Rites an. Customs p.. 107-27; Wint., HIL. I. p.. 536-44; H. H. Wilson, Viṣṇu-purāṇa. Punthi Pustak, Calcutta, 1972. p.. xvii-xx; A. Chatterjee, Padma-purāṇa-A Study; available in two recensions -- Devanāgarī an. Bengal; Kriyāyogasārafound in the ptd. edns. of Veṅk. Press an. Gurumaṇḍala Ser. is a. separate section appended to Padmapurāṇa; [Page133-b] the popularity of Rāma legend in Padmapurāṇa appears to have influenced the Jains for composing the Paumacariu or Padmapurāṇa wherein Rāma is named a. Padma.
On its relation with different texts see Antonius Edmundus Wollheim, D. nonnullis Padmapurani capitibus scriptio inauguralis quam. Berolini, 1831.
